c.tagline: The Silk Road's blue-domed jewel, capital of Timur's empire.

taxi.fareNote: Most taxis are unmarked private cars with no meter; agree the fare before getting in, or use the Yandex Go app for a fixed, fair price. Rides across the city are very cheap.

emergency.note: Dial 101 for fire, 102 for police and 103 for ambulance; 112 also works as a unified emergency number.

avoid.reason: Expect taxi overcharging and souvenir hard-selling around the Registan and Siyob Bazaar; agree prices before rides or purchases.

hood_desc: The monumental heart of Samarkand around Registan Square's three tiled madrasas, with Gur-e-Amir (Timur's tomb) a short walk away; the classic first-timer base, ringed by boutique hotels and B&Bs within walking distance of the icons.

The leafy pedestrian avenue (Universitet Xiyoboni) lined with cafes, fountains, hotels and restaurants connecting the old city to the modern town; a convenient, lively, walkable base with the widest choice of dining.

The atmospheric old-town quarter around the colossal Bibi-Khanym Mosque and the bustling Siyob Bazaar, with the tiled Shah-i-Zinda necropolis nearby; best for market life, street food and being steps from the sights.

A large modern tourism complex and eco-park about 7 km east of the old city, built around the rowing canal and its artificial lake, with international four- and five-star hotels, the Eternal City heritage park, a spa and conference venues; suits travelers wanting polished resort comfort over old-town character.
A quieter modern residential district with everyday shops, local restaurants and mid-range hotels away from the tourist core; suits longer stays and budget travelers wanting a calmer, local base.

water.note: Stick to bottled or boiled water; tap water is not reliably potable.

transit.hours: Buses and marshrutka minibuses run roughly 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM; Yandex Go taxis fill the late-night gaps.
transit.note: Samarkand has no metro or tram; travel is by city buses, shared marshrutka minibuses and cheap taxis (book via Yandex Go for a fixed fare). The major monuments cluster within a walkable historic core.
transit.pay: Bus fares are paid in cash or by Uzcard/Humo card to the driver (about 1,700 so'm). Taxis are cheap; agree the fare in advance or use the app.

bus: Intercity buses & shared taxis to Bukhara, Tashkent and Shakhrisabz
train: Afrosiyob & Sharq trains (Samarkand station) to Tashkent, Bukhara and Khiva

transit.m: City bus / marshrutka minibus to the center (~30 min)
Taxi or Yandex Go to the center (15-20 min)

tip.r: Not expected; upscale restaurants may add a 10-15% service charge, otherwise rounding up the bill is enough.

food.name: Plov
food.desc: Samarkand-style pilaf, layered rather than stirred: rice, yellow carrot, chickpeas and lamb built in a cauldron and served at midday.

food.desc: Hand-pulled wheat noodles in a peppery lamb and vegetable broth, or fried dry with tomato and capsicum. Central Asian comfort food.

places.name: Shokhrukh Nur

landmarks: Registan Square
Three colossal turquoise-tiled madrasas frame Central Asia's most magnificent plaza, a Silk Road showpiece that dazzles by day and glows under evening illuminations.
Shah-i-Zinda Necropolis
A narrow avenue of mausoleums cloaked in the finest blue tilework in the Islamic world, climbing a hillside sacred since the 11th century.
Gur-e-Amir Mausoleum
The ribbed azure dome sheltering Tamerlane's jade tomb inspired the Taj Mahal and remains Samarkand's most elegantly proportioned monument.
Bibi-Khanym Mosque
Built by Tamerlane to be the Islamic world's largest mosque, its monumental 35-metre portal still overwhelms visitors five centuries after construction.
Ulugh Beg Observatory
The excavated underground arc of a gigantic 15th-century sextant reveals how Tamerlane's astronomer-grandson charted the stars with astonishing precision.
Siyob Bazaar
Samarkand's sprawling main market heaps golden bread, dried fruit and spices beneath awnings in the photogenic shadow of Bibi-Khanym's domes.
Afrasiyab Settlement & Museum
The grassy mounds of ancient Samarkand hide 2,500 years of history, with the museum's 7th-century Sogdian frescoes as the star exhibit.
Hazrat Khizr Mosque
A jewel-box hilltop mosque with a carved painted veranda offering sweeping views over Bibi-Khanym, Shah-i-Zinda and the old city.
Mausoleum of Saint Daniel (Khoja Daniyar)
Pilgrims of three faiths visit this riverside shrine, where a legendary 18-metre sarcophagus is said to hold relics of the prophet Daniel.
Konigil Meros Paper Mill
A watermill village workshop where artisans revive Samarkand's medieval craft of silky mulberry-bark paper, once prized across the Silk Road.

train.note: Samarkand station is a few kilometres northwest of the Registan and is the busiest stop on the high-speed line: Afrosiyob trains reach Tashkent in a little over two hours and Bukhara in about 1.5 hours, with slower Sharq and Nasaf services and overnight trains running west to Urgench and Nukus. Booking opens 60 days ahead on eticket.railway.uz and the Afrosiyob regularly sells out, so reserve as early as you can; you need your passport to get into the station and to board. Uzbekistan Railways' international trains to Kazakhstan and Russia are timetabled out of Tashkent rather than Samarkand, so a cross-border rail journey starts with a domestic hop to the capital.

bus.note: There is no scheduled international coach network. The usual way into Tajikistan is a shared taxi or marshrutka to the Jartepa/Sarazm border post about 45 minutes west, then another car on to Panjakent or Dushanbe; the crossing is open to most nationalities and takes an hour or so. Domestically, shared taxis and minibuses leave the Ulugbek and Registan bus stands for Tashkent (about 4 hours), Bukhara (about 4 hours) and Shakhrisabz, departing when full and paid in cash som.

ferry.note: Samarkand lies inland in doubly landlocked Uzbekistan with no navigable river or lake nearby, so there are no passenger boats.

half.name: Urgut
half.blurb: A sprawling weekly bazaar in the foothills east of Samarkand trades wool, dried fruit, and hand-forged knives from surrounding villages.

full.name: Shakhrisabz
full.blurb: Timur's hometown holds the ruined Ak-Saray Palace gate and the Kok Gumbaz mosque, reached over a mountain pass south of Samarkand.

full.name: Nurata
full.blurb: A desert town with pre-Islamic fortress ruins attributed to Alexander the Great and a sacred spring said to hold trout that predict fortune.
